gukey: Reporting in the past: the verb takes a step back
o0ka4l: When you report today what someone said at another time, the reporting verb is in the past (“dijo”, “contó”, “explicó”) and the verb of the quote usually moves back one tense. “Tengo prisa” becomes “dijo que tenía prisa”; “Ya lo pagué” or “Ya lo he pagado” becomes “dijo que ya lo había pagado”; “Volveré el viernes” becomes “dijo que volvería el viernes”.
101mt56: The imperfect does not change (“Antes vivía en Cholula” → “dijo que antes vivía en Cholula”). If what was said is still true now or hasn’t happened yet, you can keep the original tense: “Me dijo que el taller abre a las nueve” (and it still opens at nine).
1lp7qbf: Before reporting, ask yourself: is what they said still true today? If not, move the verb back.
ak2l2u: What they said → what you report
wvoh8y: Sunday has already passed: the future in the quote becomes conditional.
dzznjj: Who, where, when: references change too
95e60n: When you report, you change the point of view. “Mi taller” in the teacher’s mouth is “su taller” in yours; “aquí” may become “allí”; “hoy” becomes “ese día”, “mañana” becomes “al día siguiente” and “ayer” becomes “el día anterior”, if you are no longer on that day.
1w2xc9r: Questions are reported without question marks. If the question is answered with yes or no, use “preguntó si”: “¿Hacen envíos?” → “Preguntó si hacíamos envíos”. If it has a question word, you repeat it with its accent: “¿Cuánto cuesta?” → “Preguntó cuánto costaba”. For requests, use “me pidió que” or “me dijo que” with three forms learnt as a chunk: “viniera”, “llamara”, “hiciera” (if you speak to someone as tú: “vinieras”, “llamaras”, “hicieras”).
1myav3k: “I’ll bring the design tomorrow.” → She said she was bringing the design the next day.
3dz4o9: “Do you use lead-free paint?” → He asked me whether we used lead-free paint.
9b1tj6: “Where is the shop?” → She wanted to know where the shop was.
13ojkjx: “Call me on Wednesday.” → She asked me to call her on Wednesday.
1608vjj: “Come early.” → The teacher told me to come early.
49vkw: “Si” only goes with yes/no questions; with “cuándo” it isn’t needed.
jn4i2p: A request reported in the past takes “hiciera”, not the present indicative.
1nn10dj: “Se” that agrees with the thing: se vende, se venden
ppdiny: When it doesn’t matter who does something, but what is done, you use “se” + a third-person verb. The verb agrees with the thing: “Se pinta cada plato a mano”, “Se pintan los platos a mano”. It’s what you see on signs and adverts: “Se vende local”, “Se reparan bicicletas”.
9jw0u8: If the thing is not specific, it goes without an article and without “a”: “Se buscan aprendices” (any apprentices). It works in every tense: “El taller se fundó en 1924”, “Las piezas se entregarán en marzo”.
wb4mx1: The verb looks at the thing
1d12wep: “Azulejo” is singular: so is the verb.
25nfrw: When there is no thing to agree with, the verb is always singular: “En Puebla se come muy bien”, “En el taller se trabaja en silencio”, “Se prohíbe tocar las piezas”, “Se dice que la talavera llegó de España”. With specific people “a” appears and the verb stays singular: “Se busca a los dueños del perro”.
1dlpq7u: There are other ways of not saying who: the third person plural (“Dicen que va a llover”, “Me cobraron de más”) and “uno”, which is required with verbs that already carry “se”: “Al principio uno se cansa mucho”.
uat8ai: Look for the thing: if there is a noun without “a” before it, the verb agrees with it; if there isn’t, singular.

2bqwjc: Direct question and reported question: the intonation changes
bbolz1: A direct yes/no question ends with a rising tone: “¿Hacen envíos?”. When you report it (“Preguntó si hacían envíos”), it’s no longer a question but information: the sentence ends with a falling tone, like any statement.
cw3b3y: Something similar happens with a question word: in “¿Cuándo abren?” the stress is on “cuándo”; in “Quería saber cuándo abrían”, “cuándo” keeps its stress, but the sentence ends falling. If you raise your tone at the end when reporting, it sounds as if you were the one asking.
mxeoc4: In the reported question the “¿?” marks disappear, but the question word keeps its accent: “preguntó qué quería”, “no sé dónde vive”. “Si” in “preguntó si” has no accent.
1nf34zi: Rise at the end of the question; fall at the end of the reported sentence.

uhuste: This is how a piece is made at Casa Pájaro Azul
u5c9dw: The workshop where Ximena works explains on its page how its pieces are made and collects what some visitors tell it.
1nq87z1: At Casa Pájaro Azul talavera is made as it was a hundred years ago. The clay is brought from two mines near Puebla and mixed by hand. Then it is left to rest for about three months, because that makes it easier to work. The pieces are shaped on the wheel or in moulds and dried in the shade for several weeks.
hb8on7: Then they are fired for the first time and covered with a white glaze. On that base the design is drawn with a paper stencil and painted by hand with donkey-hair brushes. Only six traditional colours are used. Finally, each piece is fired again and checked one by one: if a flaw is found, it is not sold as a first-quality piece.
f60qr6: In the workshop nobody works in a hurry, and it shows. Many visitors tell us so. A teacher from Oaxaca told us she had bought her first cup here thirty years before and still used it every morning. A Japanese student asked us whether he could stay for a week to learn, and we told him to come back in summer. Last week a little girl wanted to know why the plates were so expensive. We explained how many hands touch each piece, and her dad told us he would never haggle at a market again.
ziia8m: Visits are accepted from Tuesday to Saturday. Please arrive on time and do not touch the pieces that are drying.
